subject: Immunology
vignette: A 51-year-old woman has a renal transplant and is maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate. Six years after transplantation she is found to have multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and a rapidly enlarging lymph node. Biopsy of the node shows large atypical lymphoid cells that are positive for Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA (EBER).
question: Which of the following best explains the increased risk of this post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder?

options.text: Impaired NK cell-mediated recognition of missing MHC class I
Loss of MHC class I expression on the EBV-infected B cells
Loss of T-cell-mediated immune surveillance against virally infected B cells
Increased expression of tumor antigens due to chronic inflammation
Defective complement fixation by tumor-bound IgM

explanation_correct: The immunosuppressive drugs used after transplantation weaken T-cell-mediated immune surveillance, allowing proliferation of EBV-infected B cells that would normally be eliminated by cytotoxic T lymphocytes. EBV drives B-cell proliferation and immortalization, so unchecked infection progresses to post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder. The same failure of surveillance underlies the markedly increased risk of virally driven cancers, especially cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, in transplant recipients.

explanation_incorrect.A: NK cells do kill cells with absent MHC class I, but this disorder arises from loss of cytotoxic T-cell control of EBV-infected B cells rather than from NK deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.B: EBV-driven B-cell proliferation does not depend on loss of MHC class I; the tumor cells usually retain class I and are controlled by T cells that are pharmacologically suppressed.
explanation_incorrect.D: Chronic inflammation can promote carcinogenesis, but the direct driver here is EBV infection without T-cell control.
explanation_incorrect.E: Complement and IgM antibodies are not the principal defense against EBV-infected cells, and no such defect is created by these drugs.

educationalObjective: Immunosuppression impairs T-cell immune surveillance, allowing EBV-driven B-cell proliferation and virally associated cancers to escape control.
source: Generated from 2. Immunology.pdf - Tumor Immunology: Immune surveillance and tumor evasion

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history undergoes resection of a poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma. Pathology reports that the tumor cells have lost immunohistochemical staining for MHC class I molecules while retaining normal numbers of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. Postoperative staging is otherwise unremarkable.
question: Loss of MHC class I on these tumor cells most directly impairs which of the following?

options.text: Recognition of tumor peptides by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
Recognition of tumor antigens by CD4+ helper T cells
Phagocytosis of antibody-coated tumor cells
Activation of the classical complement pathway
Generation of inflammatory mediators by neutrophils

explanation_correct: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognize tumor peptides presented on MHC class I and destroy the presenting cell. Downregulation or loss of class I therefore provides a direct escape from T-cell-mediated killing and is a common tumor evasion strategy. Such cells can still be attacked by NK cells, which kill targets lacking class I MHC because inhibitory KIR receptors are no longer engaged, unless the tumor also upregulates class I-like ligands such as HLA-G or sheds soluble NKG2D ligands.

explanation_incorrect.B: CD4+ helper T cells recognize peptides on MHC class II, not class I, so their antigen recognition is not directly affected by this change.
explanation_incorrect.C: Phagocytosis of opsonized cells depends on Fc receptors and complement receptors and does not require tumor MHC class I expression.
explanation_incorrect.D: Classical complement activation requires antibody binding to antigen, not presentation of peptides on MHC molecules.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neutrophil inflammatory mediator release is independent of tumor MHC class I expression and is not the step blocked here.

educationalObjective: Tumors escape CD8+ T-cell killing by downregulating MHC class I, which simultaneously makes them more susceptible to NK cell attack.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 47-year-old woman undergoes wide local excision of a 3.2 mm nodular melanoma. Immunohistochemistry of the tumor reveals dense infiltration by CD25+ FOXP3+ lymphocytes that suppress neighboring effector cells. Serum analysis also shows elevated transforming growth factor beta and interleukin-10.
question: This tumor is most likely evading immune destruction through which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Defective antigen processing by tumor proteasomes
Induction of broadly suppressive regulatory T cells
Reduced expression of MHC class I on tumor cells
Decreased expression of costimulatory B7 molecules on dendritic cells only
Absence of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes

explanation_correct: Many tumors recruit and expand CD4+ CD25+ FOXP3+ regulatory T cells, which suppress effector T-cell proliferation and cytokine production and secrete immunosuppressive cytokines such as TGF-beta and IL-10. The result is a locally tolerant tumor microenvironment that permits tumor growth despite the presence of lymphocytes. Regulatory T cells also explain why high Treg density correlates with an unfavorable prognosis in several solid tumors, and they are a target of investigational therapies such as low-dose cyclophosphamide and anti-CCR4 antibodies.

explanation_incorrect.A: Antigen processing defects would present differently, with reduced peptide display and absent T-cell influx, rather than a dense suppressive Treg infiltrate.
explanation_incorrect.C: MHC class I loss would reduce CD8+ T-cell attack but would not explain the CD25+ FOXP3+ infiltrate or the elevated TGF-beta and IL-10.
explanation_incorrect.D: Loss of costimulation on dendritic cells alone would not account for the described intratumoral Treg population and the associated suppressive cytokines.
explanation_incorrect.E: The biopsy explicitly shows numerous tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, contradicting this option.

educationalObjective: Tumors evade immunity by recruiting FOXP3+ regulatory T cells, whose TGF-beta and IL-10 secretion creates a locally immunosuppressive microenvironment.
source: Generated from 2. Immunology.pdf - Tumor Immunology: Immune surveillance and tumor evasion

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 62-year-old woman has a node-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast treated with lumpectomy and radiation. Her tumor is biopsied decades later at recurrence; the recurrent cells show markedly reduced expression of MHC class I molecules compared with the original tumor, yet they grow rapidly. Flow cytometry of the recurrent cells reveals abundant surface HLA-G, which engages inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells.
question: Which of the following best explains why these MHC class I-deficient tumor cells are not eliminated by natural killer cells?

options.text: NK cells require MHC class I molecules to become activated
HLA-G delivers an inhibitory signal to NK cells, mimicking normal self-MHC
NK cells have been rendered anergic by chronic exposure to tumor antigens
The tumor cells secrete antibodies that neutralize NK cell Fc receptors
Loss of MHC class I prevents NK cells from recognizing the tumor as foreign

explanation_correct: NK cells kill targets that lack MHC class I because the absence of normal self-MHC disengages their inhibitory receptors, the 'missing self' hypothesis. Tumors counter this by expressing nonclassical class I molecules such as HLA-G, which bind inhibitory NK receptors (including KIR and ILT2) and replace the inhibitory signal that normal class I molecules would provide. This 'pseudo-self' masks the missing-self signal and permits continued tumor growth, illustrating how tumor evasion can co-opt either arm of the surveillance system.

explanation_incorrect.A: NK cell killing is inhibited, not activated, by engagement of their MHC class I receptors; NK cells are the cells that recognize missing self.
explanation_incorrect.C: NK cells are not the anergic cell type implicated here; classical anergy describes CD4+ T cells that receive TCR stimulation without costimulation.
explanation_incorrect.D: The tumor cells shown are not antibody-secreting plasma cells, and NK cells lack Fc receptors in the manner required for this explanation.
explanation_incorrect.E: The opposite is true: NK cells are specifically activated when MHC class I is absent, so loss of class I alone would make the tumor more vulnerable.

educationalObjective: Tumors expressing HLA-G can override the missing-self signal and suppress NK cell-mediated killing, complementing MHC class I loss as an evasion strategy.
